newsitem.title: FRANCE: French banks seen showing better 96 performance.
newsitem.headline: French banks seen showing better 96 performance.

text.p: After years of poor profits, 1996 results promise to be better for most French banks, although earnings ratios will still lag those of their U.S. and British counterparts, analysts say.

"We believe the long deterioration of results in France may be ending," said Matthew Czepliewicz of U.S. brokerage house Salomon Brothers, which has steadily raised its weighting in the entire French banking sector since last summer.
One of the biggest factors behind the change of heart on the sector has been a fall in the banks' bad-debt provisioning which weighed on results in previous years, analysts say.
Banks were hammered by a slump in property values after they and other financial institutions invested heavily in development projects just ahead of a downturn in the early 1990s.
Stronger international earnings, better returns from market activities, cost-cutting and a slightly better domestic situation are also expected to boost performance, according to analysts.
"The strong fall in interest rates certainly hurt deposit banks but it benefited market activities, which means universal banks will have done better than mutual banks," one analyst said.
Margins continued to be hit by strong competition, although some analysts detected a slight improvement in the second half of last year.

BNP, one of the Big Three commercial banks, is expected to show profits up a stunning 98 percent to 3.52 billion francs ($622 million) from 1.78 billion in 1995, according to an average compiled from forecasts by 11 Paris-based analysts surveyed by Reuters. It releases its results on March 6.

Societe Generale, another of the Big Three, is expected to report that profits climbed 21 percent to 4.65 billion francs from 3.82 billion the previous year, the analysts forecast. The bank reports on March 12.
Even Credit Lyonnais, the state-controlled bank whose expansion drive in the 1980s almost left it bankrupt, is expected to show a big rise. It announces its profits on March 20.

Analysts forecast that the bank, which the government aims to privatise in two years, helped by a third state bailout package due at the end of March, would show a profit of 150 million francs, up from a profit of 13 million the previous year.
But that profit will be thanks to the government's move to soften terms of a loan made under a 1995 state bailout to finance the spinoff of dud assets from its balance sheet.
Other factors fuelling new optimism have been strong statements by authorities over the past year pledging changes to the tight regulatory framework governing the sector.
Last week, Finance Minister Jean Arthuis promised reorganisation of the industry, including changes to a restrictive 1937 decree restricting bank opening hours.
He said an overhaul of the sector could not wait any longer if French banks were to be ready to meet the challenges posed by European monetary union, due to start on January 1, 1999.
The full-year results are expected to confirm trends shown in the first half with a rise in net banking income.
Risk costs are expected to be lower overall, although Societe Generale and Banque Nationale de Paris (BNP) still have not yet finished provisioning against real estate.

"The rising risks on small and medium-sized business...were not as bad as we feared," an analyst said. "Still, the banks will pass more provisions on small and medium-sized business to keep a margin for themselves," he said.
Leading the way for French banks, Societe Generale is expected to take a 500 million to one billion franc charge to ready itself for the switch to monetary union, analysts say.

Domestically, deposits held up well. But new loan creation was still not strong, although some banks could fare better than others such as CCF and Societe Generale, they added. ($ = 5.659 French Francs)
